                                      PROJECT NO. 58000

    RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                          §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                      §
    TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                    §
    IN THE ERCOT REGION                           §                   OF TEXAS


                 COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

                                      I.​   INTRODUCTION

         The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) represents the collective voice of more than

200 companies, representing some of the state's largest employers and energy customers. In total,

TEBA members represent more than $36 trillion in market capitalization and hundreds of

thousands of employees in Texas. Our organization is focused on helping to shape Texas'

electricity market redesign in ways that propel Texas' economy forward, lower power bills for all

energy customers, create jobs, spur innovation, strengthen the ERCOT grid, and extend Texas'

energy dominance through the energy transition and for generations to come.



      II.​     RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

     1.​ Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provision

         be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or

         different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

​            We do not view NCP as a viable solution. Maintaining the CP structure provides

essential demand response during periods of high grid usage and investment signals for

colocated generation. An NCP rate structure is at odds with the Commission’s broader objectives

and should not be explored as an option. It is not beneficial for residential customers.




                                                 1
 ​      TEBA does not have a set position on what the Minimum Billing Demand (MBD)

percentage should be. However, our study filed on July 30th (Project No. 58000, Item 12)

indicates that a flat MBD of 75% for 13 years or 80% for 9 years on new large loads ensures they

cover their incremental transmission costs while putting downward pressure on existing

customers’ transmission rates.

​      But, TEBA understands that there are trade-offs to balance, and adjustments may need to

be considered to the structure of the MBD to make it workable for large traditional loads. The

most straightforward approach would be to set a different MBD for large loads above a certain

higher threshold than 75 MW. We do, however, caution the use of this. At times, setting a MW

threshold creates a “target to avoid” – if the threshold is set at 250 MW, then loads will develop

to be as big as they can without passing that 250 MW threshold.



    2.​ Should the large load minimum billing demand be:

           a.​ Fixed for 20 years as proposed;

           b.​ Reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

           c.​ Extended to a longer time period?

​      As outlined in TEBA’s July 30th filing, we commissioned an independent study to

evaluate the appropriate design and rates for the minimum billing demand.

​      The results from our study do not justify a billing demand that is fixed at 100% for a

20-year term. Our data instead indicates that a MBD requirement of 80% for 9 years protects

existing customers while preserving the rate-reducing benefits of large load growth. The

conclusions of our study suggest that the PFP’s proposal of 100% MBD for 20 years would

significantly overcollect against the revenue requirement. For example, our study found that



                                                2
 setting the MBD at 100% for 5 years would overcollect $1.5 billion above the revenue

requirement, which is inconsistent with cost causation principles (see chart below).




 Source: Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region, Docket 58000,
Texas Energy Buyers Alliance, Item 12: Void letter for item 11 and Large Load Minimum Billing Demand Study, (July 30, 2026).

Additionally, setting the MBD at too high a level risks discouraging new large load

interconnections altogether. TEBA believes the Commission should be focused on maximizing

the number of large loads that connect and become paying contributors to system costs, and an

MBD calibrated at an appropriate level is more likely to achieve that outcome than a higher

MBD that risks driving load development away entirely.

​        TEBA recommends a minimum billing demand threshold of 80% and an obligation term

of 9 years. This calibration reflects the actual revenue requirements without imposing costs

beyond what is necessary to make the utility whole. TEBA’s study also demonstrates that this

level puts downward pressure on transmission costs for all existing customers. To the extent the

Commission considers alternative structures, a ratchet design that starts about 80% and steps

                                                             3
 down over time would be preferable to simply extending a flat obligation term, so long as it

remains calibrated to the actual revenue requirement. We want to note, however, that a

significantly longer obligation period may not serve the public interest once the time value of

money is taken into consideration. A dollar received today is worth more than a dollar received

in the future. Considering this, revenue collected in year 9 is more valuable, in present-value

terms, than revenue collected beyond that. As a result, extending the term past where the

incremental cost has been recovered would not necessarily create the value that the Commission

aims to capture through this policy, despite a longer term appearing more protective to other

consumers.



   3.​ Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of

       demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example,

       should the large load minimum billing demand:

          a.​ Reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing

              demand is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or

              maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet

              percentage decline in phases over the years, and how?

          b.​ Be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the

              large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large

              load customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the

              previous year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the

              percentage weighting towards contract peak demand or NCP demand

              decline in phases over the years, and how?



                                              4
 ​      TEBA reiterates the importance of preserving the CP methodology as the basis for

transmission cost allocation because of the value that the voluntary demand response component

provides. Demand response is a valuable tool for ERCOT to preserve reliability at a lower cost,

not only during emergency conditions but in day-to-day grid operations. The CP methodology

provides measurable benefit when the grid is stressed, and eliminating it could remove the

demand response benefit entirely. As the number of CPs increase, it becomes progressively more

difficult for a large load to avoid these peaks, which in turn deflates the value of curtailment. At

some point, the cost of foregone operations will outweigh the benefit of curtailing at the right

time, which will lead loads to stop voluntary curtailment altogether. TEBA believes that any

structure that increases beyond 12CP, including the use of NCP, will greatly reduce this demand

response.

​      TEBA does not support a weighted-average MBD. A weighted-average approach

reintroduces NCP, which removes the demand-response incentive for the same reasons described

above. TEBA recognizes that a flat MBD may undercollect revenue in the early years of a large

load’s interconnection. That is why there is an obligation period, set to the number of years it

takes to recover the needed incremental revenue. A ratcheted approach could also appropriately

address this issue by starting higher and stepping down over time. TEBA would support

exploring a ratchet design further as long as it ratchets down in proportion to the revenue

requirement over time. However, given the administrative complexity of a ratcheted approach,

TEBA prefers a simple, flat MBD based on 12CP demand, consistent with the 80% MBD over a

9-year term proposed above.




                                                 5
     4.​ Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

       an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load

       Interconnection Standards) and in which 50% of greater of the demand at the site

       consists of power electronic based load, specifically computation load, such as data

       centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should

       include applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for

       large computational loads.

       TEBA recommends that the Commission avoid creating a rate classification defined by

end use. Instead of having a separate rate treatment applied just to large computational loads,

TEBA recommends that the Commission adopt a demand-based threshold instead.

Distinguishing between different end uses invites line-drawing disputes and is difficult to

administer.



    5.​ Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include

       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

       service the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

​      TEBA strongly opposes broadening the definition for transmission interconnection costs

in this way. One of the strengths of ERCOT’s current transmission cost framework is that market

participants don’t have to fight over who benefits from a given transmission line or who should

pay for it. This dispute is something that causes years of infrastructure development delay across

other states and regions. The postage stamp pricing methodology is suitable here because it

allocates transmission costs broadly across the system in proportion to overall usage, rather than

requiring a case-by-case determination of which specific loads benefit from which facilities. This



                                                6
 approach reflects that transmission investment produces systemwide reliability benefits that are

difficult to attribute to a single customer. Separately allocating the cost of a particular

transmission line would undo that benefit.

​      Postage stamp pricing is the most workable methodology because it avoids a

cost-allocation problem that arises whenever infrastructure paid for by one customer later

benefits another. When a facility is built to serve a single load, that facility is already responsible

for directly bearing the cost through their Cost in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”). But, an

important complication arises in this scenario if another load connects in a future year and

benefits from that same facility. How are costs allocated in this case, and would the new load

owe the existing load any capital? These questions can be avoided through the use of the postage

stamp pricing methodology and demonstrate why the post methodology is effective.

​      This example illustrates why the current process we have here in Texas should not be

tampered with as it will open a whole new set of issues that have the potential to create more

complex problems and delay.



    6.​ If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of

       whether the large load customer has energized or if fully using available capacity,

       how should their loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and

       assessments and transmission planning studies?

​      TEBA believes that reserved transmission capacity should be reflected in resource

adequacy reports, assessments, and transmission planning studies, because it represents the load

the system is planning to serve. Reserved capacity is essential to how large load customers plan




                                                  7
 projects that individually cost tens of billions of dollars, and excluding that reserved capacity

from planning studies would understate the load ERCOT needs to prepare for.

       TEBA agrees that planning for loads that have not energized could be problematic if the

costs of this infrastructure development are passed down to other consumers. With that said, we

believe the risk is likely to be smaller in practice than originally assumed. Given the volume of

demand currently seeking to interconnect to the ERCOT grid, it’s expected that any site with

existing transmission infrastructure and available capacity will become incredibly valuable and

will be sought after by developers. This demand will substantially mitigate the possibility of

stranded assets.

       In addition, TEBA recommends that customers who determine they are unable to ramp

into their reserved capacity be permitted to voluntarily relinquish that capacity, with appropriate

advance notice to ERCOT and the relevant TSP. ERCOT or the TSP could then reallocate the

released capacity, either by adding it to an upcoming interconnection batch or remarketing it

directly. This voluntary mechanism gives customers an orderly way to give back capacity they

no longer need, and prevents the alternative in which customers over-request capacity and a

secondary market emerges for deciding who receives it.

​      We also note that this issue is closely related to ongoing conversations related to capacity

reallocation for loads that do not meet their requested capacity by a certain point in time (Iin

Project No. 58481). We encourage the Commission to consider these two issues together as part

of a single, coordinated framework.




                                                8
                                    III.​   CONCLUSION

       TEBA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

continuing to work with Commission staff on this matter.




                                                   Respectfully submitted,

​                                                  /s/ Bryn Baker
​                                                  Bryn Baker
​                                                  Texas Energy Buyers Alliance
                                                   bbaker@txenergybuyers.org

                                   PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                           §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                       §
TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                     §
IN THE ERCOT REGION                            §                OF TEXAS


      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

 ●​ TEBA recommends preserving a portion of the bill calculated by a 12CP methodology
    and rejecting NCP-based approaches as it would weaken demand-response incentives.

 ●​ TEBA’s study does not support a 100% MBD for 20 years, which could result in revenue
    collections well above the incremental revenue requirement, and instead recommends a
    MBD of 75% for 13 years or 80% for 9 years for new large loads.

 ●​ TEBA would support exploring a ratchet design further as long as it ratchets down in
    proportion to the revenue requirement over time. Given the administrative complexity of
    a ratcheted approach, TEBA prefers a simple, flat MBD based on 12CP demand.

 ●​ TEBA recommends demand-based thresholds rather than end-use-based rate
    classifications to avoid unnecessary administrative complexity and line-drawing disputes.

 ●​ TEBA opposes expanding transmission interconnection costs to projects identified
    through batch studies and supports retaining postage-stamp pricing and existing CIAC
    treatment.

 ●​ TEBA recommends including reserved transmission capacity in resource adequacy,
    transmission planning, and related assessments, while recognizing the need to manage
    potential stranded infrastructure costs.

 ●​ TEBA recommends allowing customers to voluntarily relinquish unused reserved
    capacity with appropriate notice and coordinating this framework with the Commission’s
    ongoing efforts in related proceedings.
